st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: Browning’s survey directly supports the cluster’s principal descriptive proposition: courts materially diverge among verification-only, disclosure-and-certification, and prohibition approaches, while consistently retaining human responsibility for filings. The source reports these regimes without endorsing one or supplying independent evidence of their effectiveness.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: Browning supports the cluster’s central distinction between permissible AI assistance and lawyers’ continuing responsibility for accurate filings. The article also aligns with the cluster’s account that post-discovery candour and correction affect judicial responses, while treating AI-specific certification as debatable because existing sanctions rules already govern inaccuracies, subject to added concerns about self-represented litigants.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision

kp.k: AI augments practice without transferring professional responsibility
kp.d: Browning argues that automating repetitive, less sophisticated tasks can allow lawyers to concentrate on complex strategic work, but lawyers remain accountable for competence, confidentiality, supervision, candor and independent judgment. He recommends augmentation rather than treating AI output as finished legal work.
qs: Generative AI should only be used to augment a lawyer’s work, not to replace that lawyer’s own independent judgment and expertise.
Real lawyers, however, do take a very real oath and are very much subject to discipline for their professional misconduct.

kp.k: Reported adoption expectations contain an internal numerical discrepancy
kp.d: The abstract reports that seventy-four percent of surveyed attorneys expect AI integration within the next year and says understanding is significantly lower. The introduction instead attributes to Wolters Kluwer’s 2023 survey seventy-three percent expecting integration within twelve months and the same percentage claiming understanding. Separately, the article reports that seventy-six percent of judges in a National Judicial College survey had never tried generative AI and another seven percent had tried it with a negative experience. These are reported survey responses, not demonstrated competence.
qs: seventy-three percent—claim to understand AI and how it can be applied to their work.
seventy-six percent of judges surveyed admitted they had never tried generative AI

kp.k: Fabricated authorities expose verification and candor failures
kp.d: The article uses Mata v. Avianca and People v. Crabill as examples of lawyers submitting fabricated authorities and then aggravating their failures through misleading conduct. Browning reports that Mata resulted in $5,000 sanctions against each lawyer and additional remedial requirements. He reports that Crabill was fired in July 2023 and suspended on November 22, 2023, for one year and one day for violations involving competence, diligence, candor and dishonesty. The author interprets these incidents as professional failures rather than technology alone causing misconduct.
qs: existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys to ensure the accuracy of their filings
it is inaccurate to describe this as a failure of technology; it is a failure of character.
ChatGPT did not keep Crabill from fulfilling his ethical obligations

kp.k: Supervision failures extend beyond inexperienced lawyers
kp.d: Browning rejects youth or digital familiarity as a sufficient explanation for misuse. In the Dennis Block matter, the article reports a $999 sanction for a filing containing fabricated cases; the firm blamed a departed first-year lawyer using online research, while AI involvement remained suspected. In Ex parte Lee, the court inferred possible AI preparation from nonexistent authorities and illogical briefing, denied review for inadequate briefing, and declined disciplinary referral. These examples support the author's emphasis on supervision and responsibility across seniority levels.
qs: rife with inaccurate and false statements.
it appears that at least the ‘Argument’ portion of the brief may have been prepared by artificial intelligence (AI).
the abdication—in both cases—of an attorney’s ethical obligation to supervise those junior to her.

kp.k: Client-supplied AI research also requires lawyer verification
kp.d: In the Michael Cohen matter, Browning reports that replacement counsel discovered unverified authorities and alerted the court. Cohen’s declaration said he supplied citations generated by Google Bard without understanding its generative nature, and his lawyer incorporated them without checking their existence. The example illustrates that responsibility to verify persists when purported research originates with a client.

Consistent with my ethical obligation of candor to the Court, I advised Judge Furman of this issue.

kp.k: AI-assisted advocacy raises unresolved malpractice and consent questions
kp.d: Browning recounts Pras Michel’s October 2023 new-trial motion alleging ineffective assistance involving an AI-assisted closing argument, factual confusion, missed defense opportunities and counsel’s undisclosed financial interest in EyeLevel.AI. These were allegations, not established findings; the article says no ruling had yet occurred. EyeLevel denied the financial-interest allegation and defended its tool as assistance to human decision-making. Browning raises, rather than resolves, questions about client agreement, disclosure to the judge and potential malpractice liability.

We view our technology as an AI that helps human lawyers make human decisions.

kp.k: Court responses create heterogeneous AI compliance obligations
kp.d: The article surveys 2023 judicial responses ranging from verification reminders to disclosure, certification and outright bans. Judge Starr required certification of nonuse or human accuracy checking; Judge Vaden emphasized confidentiality and identification of AI-generated text. Other judges banned AI drafting or relied on existing responsibility rules. The Fifth Circuit provision described in the article was a November 2023 proposal, with comments accepted until January 4, 2024, not an adopted rule. Browning argues that differing requirements can burden lawyers and confuse compliance.
qs: Use of artificial intelligence automated drafting programs, such as Chat GPT, is prohibited.
Some courts simply ban the use of generative AI, while others occupy various spots along a spectrum of compliance.
Courts require different types of certification, focusing on different concerns.

kp.k: Disclosure requirements may discourage beneficial technology adoption
kp.d: Browning reports concerns that compelled disclosure could deter use of specialized legal tools and become difficult to administer as AI enters search engines and standard software. He questions whether disclosure and certification duplicate Rule 11 and intrude on work product or strategy. His discussion presents specialized tools as designed to avoid hallucinations, rather than supplying comparative performance evidence proving that they do.
qs: it may be difficult for lawyers to even discern whether they have used generative AI.
Even if lawyers are aware that they are using generative AI tools, it may eventually become unreasonable to expect them to verify every generative AI output.
a solution in search of a problem?

kp.k: Firm policies and insurers influence early adoption
kp.d: The article cites a 2023 Thomson Reuters Institute report in which more than eighty percent of respondents saw legal applications for generative AI but only three percent acknowledged use at their own firms. Eighty percent of partners or managing partners reported firm risk concerns, compared with forty-four percent of associates. Browning contrasts publicized deployments with restrictive firm policies and an ALAS insurer advisory cautioning against use. He recommends policies covering education, verification, client awareness and consent, and continuing technological competence.
qs: only three percent acknowledged any generative AI use at their own firms.
An appropriate generative AI use policy should reinforce attorneys’ ethical obligations
Attorneys must still be responsible for reviewing and approving all documents generated with the assistance of AI.

kp.k: Taskforces emphasize education and human oversight
kp.d: Browning describes MIT, Texas, New York and ABA taskforces developing principles or recommendations during 2023. MIT’s proposed principles include confidentiality, competence, notice and consent, loyalty, regulatory compliance and human oversight. The Texas taskforce, chaired by Browning, recommended one mandatory technology-education hour within continuing legal education and an ethics opinion. The ABA taskforce’s remit included AI governance, legal education, risk and access to justice; these were areas for investigation rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Duty of Accountability and Supervision to maintain human oversight over all usage and outputs of AI applications.

kp.k: Florida guidance applies existing duties to AI use
kp.d: As presented in the article, Florida’s Proposed Advisory Opinion 24-1 recommends precautions against confidentiality breaches and informed consent before third-party AI use involving disclosure of confidential information. It requires review comparable to supervision of nonlawyer assistants and warns against delegating functions requiring a lawyer’s judgment and participation. Its advertising guidance permits AI-related claims but conditions superiority claims on objective verifiability. Browning discusses this as proposed advisory guidance, not a new generally applicable AI statute.
qs: a lawyer must always review the work product of a generative AI just as the lawyer must do so for the work of nonlawyer assistants such as paralegals.
obtain the affected client’s informed consent prior to utilizing a third-party generative AI program if the utilization would involve the disclosure of any confidential information
unless the claims are objectively verifiable.

kp.k: Efficiency cannot justify inflated hourly billing
kp.d: Florida’s proposed opinion, as reported by Browning, allows charging reasonable time for case-specific research and drafting with AI but warns against falsely inflating time, separately charging costs already treated as overhead, or billing clients for learning basic AI competence. The article connects efficiency to reasonable-fee obligations without predicting a general shift to fixed or value-based pricing.
qs: this increase in efficiency must not result in falsely inflated claims of time
the lawyer should be careful not to charge for the time spent developing minimal competence in the use of generative AI.

kp.k: Ethical competence extends to bias and judicial use
kp.d: Browning describes California’s November 2023 practical guidance as applying confidentiality, competence, diligence, supervision, candor and fee duties to AI, while also addressing compliance with law and discrimination risks. Michigan Judicial Ethics Opinion JI-155, issued in October 2023, addresses judges’ technological competence and risks to integrity and impartiality, including bias in algorithms or training data. Michigan does not endorse a single judicial regulatory response.

kp.k: General-purpose model findings support caution, not universal error rates
kp.d: Browning cites the 2024 Stanford study Large Legal Fictions by Matthew Dahl, Varun Magesh, Mirac Suzgun and Daniel E. Ho. The article reports testing more than 200,000 legal questions on ChatGPT 3.5, PaLM 2 and Llama2, all general-purpose models, and hallucination at least seventy-five percent of the time on questions about a court’s core ruling. It also reports more mistakes on lower federal district court cases than Supreme Court cases and susceptibility to false premises. These findings concern the specified general-purpose models and tasks, not measured error rates for specialized legal research products.

kp.k: Education is preferred over additional AI-specific regulation
kp.d: Browning’s principal recommendation is ethical guidance, technological education, supervision and human understanding rather than additional inconsistent bans and disclosure requirements. He regards existing professional duties and procedural rules as the foundation for accountability and favors human-centered integration. This is the author's normative conclusion, not a demonstrated comparison of regulatory effectiveness.
qs: More education, not more regulation, is the key.
The provision of ethical guidance and education by bar association taskforces and ethics bodies is a much more prudent path
Responsible AI integration, on the other hand—a more human-centered focus—augments lawyers, the clients they serve, and the courts.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Browning presents generative AI as a means of augmenting legal work, while arguing that unverified reliance creates professional risks and that inconsistent restrictions can impede beneficial adoption.
pts.d: Browning claims that automating repetitive, less sophisticated tasks can free lawyers for complex and strategic work. He argues that relying on AI output without verification or independent judgment implicates competence, confidentiality, supervision and candor obligations. He characterizes the misconduct examples as failures of lawyers' responsibilities rather than grounds for replacing human judgment with AI. He also identifies possible malpractice exposure, presenting this as a question raised by the Pras Michel litigation rather than an established outcome. On regulation, he argues that compelled disclosure may discourage use of beneficial tools, that inconsistent court requirements create inefficiencies and confusion, and that embedding generative AI in ordinary software may make its use difficult to identify. He advocates education and ethical guidance rather than additional regulation. Separately, he reports Florida's proposed guidance that AI-generated efficiency cannot justify inflated time charges. These are augmentation and governance claims, not predictions of lawyer displacement or quantified market restructuring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article supports its claims with reported misconduct cases, adoption surveys, a study of general-purpose models, and court and ethics materials; its preferred regulatory response is an argued recommendation rather than a measured comparative finding.
pts.d: Browning discusses Mata v. Avianca, Ex parte Lee, People v. Crabill, the Dennis Block eviction litigation, Michael Cohen's filing and Pras Michel's trial. These examples concern verification failures, fabricated authorities, supervision, candor and alleged deficient representation; they do not establish population-wide incidence. AI involvement in Lee is described as suspected, and the Block discussion likewise does not establish confirmed ChatGPT use. Michel's ineffective-assistance assertions and alleged financial conflict remain allegations in the article, which reports the vendor's denial and says the new-trial motion had not been decided. The conclusion cites Dahl, Magesh, Suzgun and Ho's 2024 Large Legal Fictions study: more than 200,000 legal questions posed to ChatGPT 3.5, PaLM 2 and Llama2, with hallucinations reported at least 75% of the time for questions about a court's core ruling. This is research on general-purpose models, not the separate evaluation of specialist legal research tools. The body cites Wolters Kluwer's 2023 survey as reporting 73% expecting integration within twelve months and 73% claiming understanding; the abstract instead says 74% expected integration and a substantially lower share understood the tools. The article also cites a judicial survey reporting 76% had never tried generative AI and 7% had tried it with a negative experience. A Thomson Reuters survey supplies the contrast between perceived applicability and reported firm use. Court orders, proposed opinions and taskforce recommendations document institutional responses, but the article offers no comparative outcome study demonstrating that education outperforms disclosure mandates.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern the early adoption period of 2023–2024, with conditional predictions about increasingly embedded AI and continuing human oversight.
pts.d: Published in June 2024, the article primarily examines incidents and institutional responses from 2023 and early 2024. Its twelve-month adoption expectation belongs to the cited 2023 survey, not to a forecast made from the present date. Claims that particular courts or ethics bodies were the first or only ones to act are the article's historical descriptions. The Fifth Circuit certification rule and Florida Advisory Opinion 24-1 are discussed as proposals at the stages described, not as universal or current requirements. Browning conditions responsible adoption on lawyers understanding limitations, reviewing output, maintaining professional judgment, protecting confidentiality and supervising assistance. He predicts only conditionally that widespread integration into routine software may make exhaustive verification unreasonable; this does not negate his present recommendation to verify legal work. His suggestion that specialized or internally customized tools are more reliable is a comparative assertion, not a demonstrated guarantee of error-free performance. The Florida consent guidance he reports specifically concerns third-party AI use involving disclosure of confidential information, while his own recommended firm policy more broadly calls for client awareness and consent.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The consequences fall on practicing lawyers, supervisors, firms, clients, self-represented litigants and judges, with human professionals retaining responsibility.
pts.d: Lawyers may gain drafting and research efficiency but incur verification work, compliance burdens, sanctions, disciplinary exposure and reputational damage when they misuse AI. Both junior and experienced attorneys appear in the examples, and Browning rejects inexperience as a sufficient explanation. Supervising lawyers and firms must oversee AI-assisted work by lawyers and nonlawyers and establish appropriate policies; malpractice carriers influence adoption through risk guidance. Clients may benefit from more efficient service but face inaccurate submissions, impaired representation, confidentiality risks and improper billing. Self-represented litigants also encounter fabricated authorities and court-imposed disclosure requirements, sanctions warnings or bans. Judges face inaccurate filings, risks involving bias and confidentiality, and a continuing need for technological competence. Browning supplies no quantified prediction about employment, staffing leverage, market shares or access-to-justice gains.
